This one is tough to recommend. There isn't anything seriously wrong here, but it's also a relatively short game that still manages to wear out its welcome before the credits. I think the biggest crime The Ascent commits is prompting you to set realistic expectations and then still failing to meet them, practically a textbook case of "less than the sum of its parts". 

The first thing you'll notice is that for an action 'RPG', there are barely any meaningful modifications you can make to your character. Some basic aesthetic choices, including gender, and nothing else. No backstory, no base stats or perks, nothing to differentiate your character from any other. Does the game promise rich character choices? Not at all, but don't expect any welcome surprises here. 

Even as you continue to progress through the game and level up, you'll notice a severe lack of depth relative to the apparent complexity of the systems and menus here. There are several character stats to assign points to at each level, but if you manage to decode the needlessly vague descriptions (or simply look up build guides like most people), you'll find that there aren't so much build 'guides' as build 'guide'. There is arguably one optimal way to build your stats--perhaps two if you really want to split hairs--and once you discover this, any illusion of choice or 'role playing' basically vanishes. Armor all has fixed stats and you quickly run out of new gear to buy, same with weapons and augments. Weapon progression is linear and global (meaning if you upgrade one type of gun, any copy you pick up maintains those upgrades), so money quickly becomes completely irrelevant. There is no economy here, no consumables besides the powerups that spill out of enemies and vending machines to be instantly used, and no inventory. 

Progression is gated by the main story, your character level (which indirectly controls your health and the damage you can do) and your cyberdeck, which you again find linear upgrades to over time. Can't open an ICE 2 door? Upgrade your cyberdeck until number go up, now interact with the door to open it. There are 4 damage types, but only two classes of enemies in the game (organic and mechanical), so only two of the damage types are particularly relevant. Ballistic and energy are generally good, with ballistic being better against organics and energy better against mechanical. Digital is practically useless against organics and fire is practically useless against mechanicals, but without any way to permanently alter the type of damage each weapon does, there's no point in trying to specialize. I can't help but imagine this game could have been much more satisfying as a pure shooter without any of these vestigial systems masquerading as RPG mechanics, especially if the effort spent on them could have been deployed elsewhere.

Combat fares far better here, although again, there's a decent chance you'll tire of it before beating the game. Most weapons and abilities have a satisfying punch to them, the gorgeous explosions create gobs of debris and particles, and enemies (and unlucky NPCs caught in the crossfire) are often dismembered or even vaporized on impact. Enemy variety is quite good and forces you to dodge, maneuver, and prioritize targets effectively. That is, until you match or exceed the level of the enemies you're fighting, at which point they become cannon fodder. All areas have fixed level ranges which don't change over the course of the game, so in the second half you will be powerful to the point of tedium compared to your foes. Especially if you equip a weapon with homing bullets and an AOE augment, you can basically autopilot your way through most areas in the game. There's no need for build diversity here, even in coop, because the most effective strategy is always to kill or suppress all enemies before they reciprocate. Environmental destruction is completely aesthetic, don't expect to be strategically removing cover or flanking through exploded walls here. Finally, a couple of the most powerful weapons in the game are only found in the final missions, where you maybe have a couple of hours of gameplay left. A new game + mode was patched in after release, but offers no compelling reasons to continue besides a familiar sandbox in which to briefly play with these new toys. No new gear or weapons, no changes to the story (as far as I could tell), and minor gameplay tweaks which have a negligible effect on combat. Melee enemies get shields that absorb some damage, ranged enemies throw more grenades. I'm sure there are others, but I just couldn't be bothered to push further.

The story is barely worth mentioning. There's some neat tech behind it with the use of proceedurally generated voice lines for NPCs and a lot of conceptually interesting lore. But it doesn't say anything meaningful, and the impact on the world you're navigating is basically nonexistent. There are no choices to be made and nothing in the way of character development. One of the NPCs repeatedly complains about failing to keep a low profile when civilians die, but to zero consequence. Civilians respawn, enemies respawn, life goes on.

Finally, this game is exceptionally pretty. The artistic direction in the details and animations are absolutely awe inspiring, and on a high-end monitor or TV at max settings, there are few games that can match it (Yes, the fixed third person perspective is doing a ton of heavy lifting here, I'm not directly comparing efficiency or technical excellence). But beauty for beauty's sake is not enough to sustain a game, and while I think The Ascent's visuals will age beautifully in a broader sense, they're not enough motivation to keep playing. Especially when you reach the final tier of the world and discover that it's far smaller and less detailed or impressive than the three preceding levels, to a degree where it looks almost like a symptom of cut content.

So given everything I just wrote why would I ever recommend this game? Well, assuming your expectations are now finally set accordingly, I think there's some fun to be had here for the right person. My advice would be to look up a build guide and the locations of a few interesting weapons, then just completely ignore the RPG mechanics. Play a few of the early side missions (they get less interesting and more fetch-questy the further on the game goes) and then just cruise through the main story once without spending too much time exploring. You won't find anything interesting, trust me. If you're the type of player (like me) who needs to see what's around each corner and inside each crate, the answer is always meaningless bundles of currency or a piece of equipment you already picked up 5 hours ago. This world and the mechanics surrounding it are perfect sequel bait, perhaps with enough support this team will get the chance to make a game that isn't just competent, but surprisingly good.

As an old guy who's played a lot of video games, The Ascent did a good job of scratching that itch of living in a cyberpunk/blade runner world. The developers did a really good job with the world and the setting. It's a game that doesn't hold your hand and leaves you to it to try and figure things out for yourself, in many games I enjoy this, but in this ascent, I was a bit lost in the beginning with where to put my points. I eventually went and looked up a popular build and was thankfully able to respect my character. The problem I had with The Ascent was that it just started to feel like a chore. The quests are all the same; go here, talk to this person, kill your way to the objective, interact or kill someone, then return. For me, the story wasn't interesting enough to keep me wanting to play, the combat got pretty repetitive for me and it started to just feel like a chore.

I can't distinguish the enemies from the civilians in a firefight.

I've killed hundreds of innocent people.

Nobody cares.

I really enjoyed my time in The Ascent (22 hours as I write this). The visuals and the audio and the music are great, the story is good, and there was reasonable character progression throughout.

[h1][u]Pros:[/u][/h1]
+ Music. I may have listened to the soundtrack on Spotify (Caution: I ran the risk of a speeding ticket)

+ Sound Effects. They're good.

+ Graphics. The isometric POV worked well. Detail was packed everywhere. The dark and dirty, neon oversaturated aesthetic was exactly what I hoped for. Plus, with ray-tracing, some of the weapon effects looked absolutely amazing, especially when they reflected off puddles.

+ Story. Many reviews have pointed out that the story is generally standard for the genre. I don't play the genre a lot, so I can't exactly say, but what I can say is that the story, combined with the atmosphere, combined with the music, was really fun.

+ Length. Took me about 18 hours to finish the game. 22 hours to get all the single player achievements. Could've gone faster, could've gone slower, but it was a good pace for me and didn't overstay it's welcome.

+ NPC's. These get a specific shout-out. The crowds of bystanders really flesh out the world, and I felt kinda bad [spoiler]blowing up a bunch of sympathetic robot garbage-men[/spoiler].

[h1][u]Cons:[/u][/h1]
- RAM Bug. When I played through, there were some annoying bugs. RAM use was the worst; the first time I entered an area the game would load all the area's content, which would give me 30 seconds or so of 1 fps (I can Star Citizen at 75 fps, so it ain't my computer's fault). Once the area was loaded, no more problem. I believe this bug has been worked out.

- Load Times. Game is on an SSD, and almost the entire game could fit on my RAM, but there are pretty lengthy load times when firing up the game or loading into a new area. The load screens are nice, whether you're in the taxi or an elevator, but they wouldn't have to be if the loading was faster.

- Achievement Bug. I absolutely have completed the codex, but didn't get the achievement. I haven't played multiplayer yet, so I'm not sure if those ones work, and I haven't died 100 times, so again, not sure if it works.

- Distance/Pathfinding. Pretty much every quest is: Get a task, go to the place, do the thing, go back to the place you got the task. That's not my complaint, since that's about 99% of quests in every adventure/RPG game. The problem is that the "go to place" part typically includes running really long distances. There is some fast travel, but the points don't always get you close to where you need to be. The fast travel also costs credits, and there is a mid-game point where it goes from too expensive to justify to no longer a problem. Fast travel or not, you will be running a long way, and there isn't a great navigation system. When you're moving through a multi-level urban setting with plenty of dead ends, a simple direction-to-objective navigation system isn't always helpful.

- Difficulty Spikes. Most of the fodder along the way to an objective is manageable. There were certainly missions that were harder, but usually nothing that couldn't be fixed with gear and weapon selection. Those missions were awesome, except for the bosses. Some of the boss fights were so much harder than their missions that it was hard to put up with- looking at you [spoiler]Megarachnoid[/spoiler]. Of course, that all pretty much stopped once I went super-saiyan in, I guess, act 3.

[h1][u]50/50:[/u][/h1]
+/- Content. This seems to be a big point of contention in the negative reviews, and I do see their point. 
Any time a game gives me openness, quests, and side-quests, I have a habit of burning out on side content early on. The Ascent limited the side stuff, and tied progression to the main story pretty well, so I found that I stayed focused on the central quest line. The result, for me, was that this game encouraged me to play through it and get to the end, which I did. Of course, this meant that I didn't explore every nook and cranny of the world, which is fine because even if there was stuff to see, there wasn't always stuff to do. I mentioned that the game didn't drag on too long, but I'd have stayed longer if there was more [i]quality[/i] content. I would probably pay for DLC, and I would be pumped for a sequel.

+/- Lore. This is tied to content. There's definitely a well made world here, with a lot going on. There are references to other things in world, and there is a lot of happenings you learn about through context. I don't love heavy exposition, and [spoiler] Grateful Abbott's news program [/spoiler] is a bit much. Others have said that this game might be too ambitious, which I understand. I've got two thoughts on this: first, there is room for expansions/DLC. I would probably pay for DLC. Second, you play as a nobody, caught up in something bigger than you are, so it would make no sense for you to get intertwined with every single facet of the world. I actually have a great deal of respect for storytellers who [i]don't[/i] explore everything. I live in a pretty small town, and there are many business owners I've never talked to.

+/- Codex. If you like lore, the codex will entertain you. It goes into detail about characters, locations, enemies, all the usual stuff. Even the brands of guns and clothes. What is missing, though, is a clear explanation of things like damage interactions. The game has different types of damage and defence and whatnot, but it's never really clear how that all works. Electric definitely beats robots, heat does not. I think digital beats everything, I don't know.

[h1][u]TL:DR[/u][/h1]
For half the price of a AAA title, you get 2/3 to 3/4 of a AAA game. Ain't perfect, but worth it.

Mostly writing this review as the game currently sits at mixed, and I believe it deserves better. It's a fun game, and I find most of the negative reviews are just plain wrong. Below I will try to refute some issues people were having with the game:

[u]Bugginess:[/u]
I have played through this game twice, and have never encountered a single bug. I ran the game on a semi-high end PC however, so it could run worse on lower end computers. Also of note is that I played it solo, so I have no idea how buggy multiplayer could be. 

[u]The map sucks:[/u]
I will say, the map is kind of hard to read, but not unusable. The map is clustered and clumped, but that reflects the Mega-City you're in. It accurately indicates every nook and cranny possible, and with a game like this one, there are going to be a lot of them. This can cause a bit of confusion in the more clustered multi-level areas, but it's not hard to figure out with a little bit of thinking. Early on in the game, the map is given to you by a shady NPC who clearly doesn't care if you live or die. Later on, you find a corpse of a character that was given a map by the same NPC who died because the map he was given was completely wrong. While this doesn't excuse the decision to have a crap map, it does fill in the world and add to the atmosphere. 

[u]The FOV sucks:[/u]
There were a few reviews noting that the FOV doesn't move with your mouse. This is just dead wrong. It will not move out of combat, but will move in combat depending on what weapon you are using. It won't move at all if you're using melee, move a bit if you're using a short range weapon like the starting pistol or smg, and will move greatly if you choose to use the snipers or the high-end rifles. 

[u]Enemy spawns are bullshit:[/u]
If you aren't paying attention to how you engage enemies, this can quickly become true. The game will spawn enemies by area. If you aggro one area, all the enemies and reinforcements tied to that area will attack you. Usually this isn't an issue, but in more congested locations certain spawn areas will be very close together and it becomes easy to aggro 2 -3 times more enemies than you're capable of taking on. If this is happening to you, take a moment to note where the enemies tend to cluster, and try to take on the groups one by one. Enemies will spawn behind you, so moving is very important. 

[u]Healing is very finicky/Not enough health around:[/u]
Early game, you are doused in abundance of health drops. Mid-late game, those tend to dry up with large gaps between safe healing spaces. This mix makes it very easy to ignore the plethora of healing abilities that neatly fit into whatever type of build you're going for. It might feel bad to drop a DPS ability for a healing one, but it feels even worse dying because you're entering fights with less than max hp.

[u]It's hard to understand what damage type I should be using for which enemy:[/u]
It's actually quite easy to understand. Try shooting a guy. If the numbers are small or red, or even if your damage isn't quite there, try using a different type of weapon. You might have to change up what weapon you want to use in the middle of combat, but that's what multiple weapon slots are for.

[u]Game is very trial and error:[/u]
This is absolutely true. No refuting this. 

If you've made it this far, here's a few things newer players should know going into the game:
[list]
[*]Cover is VERY important. If you're dying a lot in an area, try to bait the enemies into an area with more cover or better angles. 
[*]Mobility is also very important. The primary gameplay loop is about creating space that you can exist in without getting your ass blasted. Make sure you're putting points into the mobility tree early, your mental will thank you.
[*]There are four damage types in this game. Physical, Energy, Pyro, and Digital. As a general rule, you should have a physical weapon in one slot, and an energy weapon in the other. That's not to say that doing otherwise is wrong, but this combo is not only the easiest to achieve, it also will make you the most effective against the greatest variety of enemies.
[*]Harder enemies can be cheesed with pyro damage, which has a chance to light an enemy on fire. When on fire, enemies lose a percentage of health, meaning even your dinky little pyro pistol can kill some of the level 30 enemeis at level 4 if you're willing to play patiently enough.
[*]Please don't dump all your stats into crit. The skill only gives you 1% crit per level, maxing out at 20%. Your total DPS will only increase by less than a percent per point.
[*]This game is absolutely balanced around multiplayer. This isn't necessarily an issue throughout most of the game, but in the final act there are two specific fights it might be good to use an ability that spawns an ally just to grab aggro and take the pressure off you for a bit. 
[/list]

[h1]Simple Action[/h1]
This is not an action RPG, it's more like an action game. While I had fun playing this on co-op, the game remains too basic to recommend. The loot is boring, skills are limited, lots of useless running from point A to B. On the positive side, the graphics are nice and I liked the story. It had potential, but this is like bread that they took out of the oven too early. I would pass on this one.

[b]Low Recommendation[/b]

The visuals are absolutely stunning, and I'd recommend the game for those alone, but there are too many bugs and most of the developers who worked on the game have left Neon Giant, so the bugs are here to stay. To name a few I've encountered playing the game alone and in co-op:

- Random crashes, both in single player and co-op.
- Textures going missing, character disappearing from screen.
- Hard-earned, unique items vanishing in co-op when changing weapons and armour (you can purchase some back, but the shop selling these items is locked behind a DLC); logging into single player doesn't bring them back. Other reviews had their entire characters deleted, and in single player and not co-op. If you're playing the game, back up your save file once in a while.
- High ping in co-op prevents you from shooting and reloading your gun, using your abilities or doing other actions. I had to play a melee-only character with a friend of mine because of this issue and felt like a cripple throughout the run, however playing with a different friend with a good connection seemed to fix these issues.

Overall, I'd be totally on board if the devs kept updating the game, fixing the bugs and releasing DLCs. However it looks like the game is left for dead and there will be no more updates for it. A shame really, this game had a lot of potential that was never realised and by now most likely never will be.

Honestly, I didn't expect this when I first launched the game:

- A rather intriguing way of delivering the story (no spoilers - those who've played will know what I mean).
- Plenty of character upgrades and a wide variety of weapons to choose from.
- An absolutely stunning visual style, polished down to the smallest detail. There were moments after battles when I just stood still and took in the environment - it's that detailed, layered, and deep.
- Well-thought-out combat, enhanced by eye-catching visual effects.
- All aspects of the game complement each other perfectly - the project feels complete and thoroughly crafted.

I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys top-down shooters and cyberpunk, and honestly to everyone else too - I'm sure each person will find something in it that clicks with them.

I was loving this game when I first started playing it. The atmosphere is absolutely stellar for an isometric action game. There's a classic, arcade-like feel to playing it, too. The "aim high/aim low" mechanic is a nice little touch. There's an impressive amount of immersion to be had with NPCs and whatnot.

So, why the negative review?

After about 10 hours on one save file, I logged back in to find that all of the cyberdecks I collected had vanished. What's a cyberdeck? Think of it as basically a lock picking tool that allows the player to open doors to get in different areas.

Essentially, a bug suddenly removed my ability to get into several doorways/tech items. Legitimately game-breaking. A hop over to Google/Reddit quickly had me realizing this is not an uncommon bug. And since these cyberdecks were looted, I tried going back to the places in the world they are found, just for good measure. Gone. 

If I learn that some of these bugs are fixed (I think the cyberdeck is one of the larger bugs), I will change my review to positive. But, as for now, I caution any potential buyers to really read through the negative reviews and see that there are some bugs large enough to merit reconsideration of purchase.

I truly mega-wanted The Ascent to be great, but I'm afraid I always have to be brutally honest with every game I review. The Ascent is a masterfully crafted Cyberpunk game in terms of AESTHETICS and ART DIRECTION. But it lacks the crucial polish everywhere else.

The game is decent, if you have the patience for it. The Ascent scores a 5/10 solo and 6/10 if you have a buddy to enjoy coop together. I wished I had a neutral button for reviewing, but as it stands it is barely a  recommendation from me, with its amazing visuals helping it to pass my rating.

Pros:

Masterfully crafted Cyberpunk aesthetic - If you are looking for the definitive looking cyberpunk game, this game fully delivers it. The Cyberpunk world in this is pulled off accurately and full of mindblowing detail. In terms of its visuals, it is a 10/10 for me.

Good sound design and soundtrack - Guns, explosions and music all sound crisps. They have a very satisfactory reverb to them. Very impressive.

Exploring via main story - Along the main story quests, it slowly introduces more and more unique Cyberpunk areas. Makes you look forward where you are going to end up or seeing next.

Cons:

Repetitive mission chain - Quests are repetitive with no real story context to it, mostly fetch me that and kill these people for me type quests.

Terrible Checkpoint System - If you die in a boss fight prepare to restart 5-10 mins earlier in the area going through the same tedious mobs over and over again to trigger the boss fights.

Not balanced for solo play - Some boss sequences are clearly meant for 2-3 players to complete, making solo experiences at times hair-pulling difficult.

No interesting characters and poor plot - Most of the cast are extremely one-noted. A lot of the cast in the game are not voice-acted as well. As for the plot, I have no idea what's going on during 80% percent of the game. 

I recommend getting it on sale and playing it coop with friends, if you are playing solo prepare to get your experience dampened. The Cyberpunk world is truly insane and impressively crafted, and if that is what only truly matters to you, then I say go ahead.

What can I say about The Accent?

It’s a game about guns, no melee, isometric camera perspective that feels amazing in 2020, redefining my expectations for an isometric-perspective RPG, shooting people, shooting machines, shooting gangsters, shooting poor people, shooting rich people, collateral damage, and getting reprimanded for aforementioned collateral damage.

Necromunda and Cyberpunk 2077’s child exploded onto the Steam store page some time ago, and I was intrigued. Personally, I am prejudiced against any game that hosts the perspective through the wrong end of a telescope, but I actually enjoy it in this game.
On controller my right thumbstick is focused only on this twinstick-like shooting formula that reminds me of my favorite 3D Contra: Neo Contra. On keyboard and mouse, I mapped a lot of shit to my mouse because who the fuck put all this shit only within range of your Index? Was it you, Skvövbjørn?
Swedish jokes aside, did you know only twelve Swedes made this game? Holy fucking shit and how, great job folks!

Game provides for some customization on-par with Oblivion, however literally all options look the same on men and women. This means no sexy armor—at least not intentionally, I really didn’t find the four-arms armor with only the T-shirt area really “sexy”, but maybe amputees are your thing?
With that in mind, you’re really only picking what gender of person is wearing this awfully short list of items to customize your character with that you’ll maybe see one day?
I’m not joking, after you get gear there’s only arms and mouth left exposed, and that’s at level 3, right before exiting the tutorial. Once you get to level 10 you start seeing more light armor, but as heavier armor is found you see way less skin—which is nice that we don’t have the legion of ultra-Chads or Amazon Chadettes with Kombat Bikinis running around at level 20 with miniguns and the minigun that shoots rockets as their secondary.
There’s a lot to customize your character with, and I wanted to get more into the story before I wrote my review because of how many options there truly are. Depending on your build or preference your armor will dictate more than just appearance, though I wish it didn’t because some armor looks sick as hell despite not providing the five points in Not-Dying my current equipped armor is granting me that I desperately need now that I’ve finally decided to turn up the game to the difficulty you should start on: Hard mode.

If you’re looking for the illusion of a challenge, go normal mode. Hard mode had no friendly fire I could see, and at ten hours I found some big fucking guns thanks to friends joining in and hacking the planet’s rare chests I’m supposed to find later.
That being said, I don’t recommend showing up in your friend’s game and power-leveling them. Instead, I think you would both enjoy it more if your high-powered friend wore the gear that looked nicest, while using the most fun/easiest guns to shoot. At that point I hope you’re still not murderlating everything in the same zipcode before your friend even has the idea to aim, if you are: dial it back and reserve yourself to stormtrooper aim and opening locked doors and chests.

The story is very fun, and likes to give you enjoyable vacations from your camera perspective that I wish—holy shit do I wish—that literally anyone else would do. I really love Wasteland 3 because I don’t have to spend every conversation looking at the Atlas for Greece, but why the fuck are two games the exceptions to this? I’m still playing top-shelf games like Divinity and Diablo. My girlfriend has even asked if I can change the camera perspective in these games, so why is this the only one she hasn’t thought looked “kinda off”?
The game knows it has these beautiful scenes, so if you’re not near one, it will slowly drag and zoom towards you anyways if you’re standing still.
Conversations with major characters are done up-close, and you can see it’s a pretty game that is choosing perspective to help alleviate that control in gameplay. Instead of controlling the camera, you control movement direction and aiming direction, like twinstick shooters. The camera reminds me of older games like Metal Gear Solid 1 and 2, and the classic Resident Evil games such as 0-CV. It works out well, and it’s never particularly frustrating, so I really enjoyed it rather than docking a point automatically. I really enjoy taking time to take screenshots in this game, and some friends have even started warning me so I can be ready. It’s a visually beautiful, and its robust and complex gameplay focused on simple mechanics and interactions make it a really fun and exciting game that I feel really excited to play again. It’s one of the few games I somewhat-preordered, and for a new IP that always makes me nervous, however I really enjoy the product I received.

My expectations weren’t very clear, if I’m being honest. Walking into this game I expected it only to have guns, take place in the future, and I think that’s it. I was initially turned off by the perspective, but I grew to like it.
I really enjoy the story, the content and how it’s told reminds me of the classic, Pre-Bethesda Fallout games in ways I enjoy. Your character is yours to make, and you’re free to do about everything except choose how a majority of the story goes. For co-op games this is a must-have for anyone who can watch you stream it and say “that looks fun” since up to four people can join and start reliving their favorite airport mission from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2.
I’m not joking, and I’d like for you to forgive yourself and allow yourself to laugh at the screams people make in advance. I don’t know who the hell made this game, but they thought of a lot, and this production and quality should be the new standard that you evaluate this genre of RPG and perspective. Aside from DX12 turning into a nuclear bomb if enabled (read the discussions, the devs even responded to my thread, so it’s not perfect and they’re working on it), my friends and I occasionally getting stuck in places we shouldn’t have been allowed to roll/phase into, or stuck in dialogue without any escape except alt+f4, it’s a very complete and polished title, and you could swear that it was made by a triple-A game studio, so great job to the developers for making such an excellent game!

TLDR: This one is imho, Criminally under-rated if you're into TDS. 

Only 6.7% of players Reset their talents and only 2.7% of players died 100 times. = Nobody really seemed to actually give this game the chance it deserved.

The graphics are phenominal, the story isn't as bad as people make it out to be. Sure, it's not shakespear but ffs it's a TDS, we're here to shoot sh1t and look good while doing it. 

I think where this game sufferes isn't by any fault of it's own but merely as a consequence of the times. Yeah, you spend the entire game traveling afoot. So in a generation raised with COD style instant action shooters where combat is never ceasing, a game like this can feel "slow". Sometimes, you really are just traveling around, taking in the sights as you traverse the outstandingly well designed environments this game has to offer, occasionally encountering groups of mobs here and there. 

But see that's where "criminally underrated" comes to fruition here. I think so many who have "played" this game have just given up on it. Hell even I had a moment where I thought "Bruh, idk man, this is kind of slow". Because you can vendor purchase most every item in the game right out the gate. So you can transmog your character to look exactly how you want it, with the weapons you desire virtually immediately. Or so I thought. 

But once I trudged through the early/mid game and began to encounter mechs and suits and all the other awesome stuff, the gear quality started to improve and the sexiest of the armors began to drop. So if anything I think this game probably turns off folks that need more than a soiid gameplay loop, but demand and insist a "reward" system of some kind to keep them playing. 

I was perfectly content playing 80% of this game with the same gear I found pretty much early game. I upgraded my equipment, transmogged to look like a badass and then just enjoyed being a merc for hire. Because the combat just feels really good to me. The sound design is spot on (if you got solid headphones or surround sound it's a MUST), and once you start playing with all the gadgets you begin to realize that movement doesn't feel near as daunting as you'd once thought. 

Look. I'm not here to hold your hand and pat your back. FFS it's on sale right now for $7.49 (I paid full price, and I don't regret it). If you just want a game you can be a badass in, with some incredible visuals and sound design, just buy it. This is not a game that requires much brain power, just spend your points in a logically balanced manner and enjoy. I played on Normal and found it moderately difficult, and having just beat it after about 40 hours (twice as long as HLTB suggests it should take), honestly I'm already eager to play New Game + on hard..... and they tease that New Game + comes with new "tricks up their sleeve".

Two important points to start with (at 7h of gameplay):
1. this is not a Diablo-like ARPG with random loot and procedurally generated dungeons. This is a story-based fixed-world twin-stick shooter with RPG elements (as in, your character has stats, but doesn't have a choice). And "fixed world" means that there is very little replayability potential. I hope I'm proven wrong by the time I finish it, but right now it seems like a one-playthrough game
2. there are bugs, sometimes game-breaking (quest target enemies didn't spawn for me on one of the story quests), there are some important QoL features missing (sprint, please?), and UI could use some polish. Devs have promised support and patches, looking forward to it

Now, to the good parts:
1. this game is a damn eye candy. The world is huge, full of amazing little details, and is absolutely gorgeous. Fantastic level design, lighting, camera angles: 10/10 GOTY on graphics alone
2. shooting is fun and complex. While the early stages you are somewhat restricted in what kind of build your character can realistically have, by mid-game the possibilities grow by a lot

Update (at 13h of gameplay):
As I keep playing, my opinion of the game keeps going down. The graphic fidelity is still undeniably there, although endless high-fidelity drab corridors with very detailed crates in them are getting somewhat old, but apart from it there aren't many areas for which I could give The Ascent praise. Sidequest design in particular is quite poor because you constantly get sent into locations that are either hard-locked behind main quest progression or are way above your level (looking at you, both stages of Anabolic Express quest). Navigation is bad because the map lacks detail (try finding a building that you don't have a marker for), map markers don't have height indication, and quests rarely tell you which fast travel location would be optimal to take. And loot system still doesn't make any sense. Why does the concept of duplicate items even exist? 

Final update (after finishing the game):
Overall, it's a good game. The plot is solid, gunplay is decent, and you've heard it all about graphics already. Here're a few tips to get the most out of the game:
1. Use the damn taxi. Don't hoard money.
2. Use the damn cover. At a certain point kiting becomes too slow and too boring.
3. Focus on the main mission. You can work on the sidequests later.

P.S.: the alphanumeric code in armor name describes its resists. E-30 Something Something gives 30 points of (E)nergy armor, PF-40 Something Something gives 40-ish points of (P)hysical and (F)ire armor.

This game was not at all what I had expected it to be. I expected it to be a sort of procedurally generated roguelike/lite where you tried to fight level to level, always climbing higher, to try to reach the top of the arcology while fighting a variety of enemies (gangers, CorpSec, mutants, robots, etc) and equipping a variety of gear in order to eventually reach the top and do... something?

What the game actually IS a a beautifully and intricately imagined crapsack sci-fi dystopian story-based game more akin to Diablo than Hades. I liked all the characters, I didn't have any gripes with the voice acting, I loved all the set pieces, and most of the guns feel sufficiently distinct from eachother that it's worth experimenting to find favorites (although it seems like some of them are better for almost all situations than others, and damage type distribution by enemy weakness seems to be a little bit skewed, but eh). The world is expansive, and rewards you for exploring by hiding various goodies and chests and rare equipment in various corners and behind various locked doors.

The story and world are immersive and intriguing, and the art and soundtrack definitely help pull you in. Gunplay is fast, snappy, and reasonably tactical. Augs and tactical/grenade abilities add another layer of customization that significantly changes combat flow.

Minus points:
- As of the current build, two cutscenes have an issue where the animations and audio are misaligned (the first encounter with Kira, and the final cutscene of the game)
- nogHead the hacker has a few lines toward the end of the game delivering exposition about what's really going on that have VERY different text from the audio delivered over that text
- In a number of cases the "recommended level" associated with many of the sidequests is seemingly arbitrary, and there are a few sidequests that actually can be picked up WELL before the location where they can be completed is unlocked
- There are hackable turrets in the game. They are never anywhere that would actually be even remotely useful, and you cannot hack a turret that has aggroed on you. There are mortar turrets that, at present, can only be destroyed with grenades or a specific augmentation that shoots rockets, but switching to those in the midst of play empties the gauges that let you even use those things

Bonus points:
- At points the game's difficulty seems to spike, though this can generally be adjusted by shifting gear around to find guns that exploit enemy weaknesses, armor that blocks enemy damage type, and grenades/augs/"tactical equipment" that can strategically turn the tide. Thats said, THE ONLY THING DYING COSTS YOU IS TIME. You don't lose XP, you don't lose money, you don't lose durability. In fact, loot picked up before death is kept, making it very easy to grind for money and xp, and potentially get some very good (and in one specific case ABSOLUTELY NECESSARY) gear.

Areas of confusion:
- Until nearly the end of the game the random bounties are all, as far as I could tell, "low grade" bounties, regardless of what level they were or how hard they hit. Every single bounty turns in for 1000 uCred regardless of what level that bounty was. More than half of the guns in this game can be sold to vendors for more than 1000 uCreds, meaning disposing of bounties is less lucrative than selling a bounty's weaponry. Weird point of worldbuilding.
- I kept expecting there to be more consequences to my inadvertent slaughter of uninvolved civilians than mild and occasional scoldings from my boss. Something like actually having corpsec, or one of those huge rocket mechs descend from the sky out of nowhere in the middle of a fight and try to ruin my day, maybe. Never happened.
- It would be cool if, after doing jobs for the Liquid Quiks, some of the "neutral" gang members hanging out in various places became allied (green) characters, in recognition of your work for/with them. Same with the Rojin. At present, that's not a thing, which lends itself well to the whole "fight your way back through this entire neighborhood because you're too cheap to call a taxi" thing, but it still feels... weird.

Altogether, I really enjoyed playing The Ascent and found it to be both a fun game and a very pretty intentionally dystopian-looking world to run around in,

It's difficult to whole-heartedly recommend The Ascent because it often seems at odds with itself.  Still, if you know what you're getting into and don't mind what it is, it's great fun.  I put in a handful of hours before I felt the need to do something else and keep in mind that I only played this solo.

Visually and aurally, this game is phenomenal.  I don't know where these guys came from, but the A/V of the Ascent is bedazzling in ways that I haven't experienced in a quite some time.  I expect this kind of stuff from the Big Three in terms of the aesthetics, but both the art and sound departments deserve all the kudos coming to them because they outdid the Big Three in a very obvious way.  There are so many details that hide the rubber stamping, as if each section of the game is hand-crafted and tailored to suit the situation.  Even the obvious "you can't go this way" walls are blended in meticulously and if ever there was a futuristic sh*thole to be put on screen, this is one of the very best representations of it.  From all the nasty details in the foreground where the action takes place to the incredible body of movement and destruction that takes place in the background, I haven't enjoyed [i]looking[/i] at a game so much in quite some time.  Aurally, the game is a wondrous cacophony of city noise, full of alien chatter, blasted announcements and vehicles whizzing by.  If you're the type of gamer that has an amazing sound set-up, be sure to use "Indent Mode" to get the most out of all the ambience they packed into each scene.  If I was judging the game on the A/V alone, I'd call it a masterpiece.

That said, it's all built around a twin-stick shooter which, by and large, is usually a wholly-accessible and mindlessly-fun genre to sink your teeth into, typically featuring you mowing down popcorn mobs in order to get to meaty boss fights.  The Ascent, on the other hand, trades popcorn mobs for bullet sponges and spaces them out in huge environments that don't seem to fit the character's move speed.  While admittedly the mobs go down easily enough, a lot of combat involves dodge-rolling to safety while you empty your gun at somewhat mindless drones that just track towards you.  It's all well and good until adds just spawn in behind you (dropped from passing vehicles, for example, or just outright appearing from off-screen) and then it gets kind of annoying.  By no means is it broken, but it just kinda takes some of the fun out of it.  Couple these bursts of actions with lots of traversing wide swaths of empty space and it quickly dwindles down to a more robotic rhythm that starts to show its limits rather quickly.  It would have gone a long way if you could self-manage your health, but such as it is, you have to go find pick-ups or wait for mobs to drop healing baubles.  To be fair, however, it's not hard to find vending machines for healing, but if you're unlucky in a firefight, you've got no way to mitigate the damage.  To be even fairer, dying isn't really an ordeal and you're placed pretty close to where you went down and whatever you killed will still be dead (if it's a unique mob, that is).

On the more crunchy side of things, the game features a stat progression and levelling system that feels significant; each level definitely makes life a bit easier - at least for a time - and how you assign your skill points feels weighty.  Sadly, there's not a whole lot to distinguish your character from the next one as there are no classes here.  You can wield any weapon (at least as far as I am into the game) and wear any armor you want.  While it's not quite a looter shooter, you will inevitably find stronger variants of everything and you can also spend precious resources to upgrade them.  While this is quite straight-forward, one of the key features is that if you dump your weapons for money, should you ever reacquire them in the field, they will retain their upgrades.  Like other games before it, however, sometimes the upgrading seems silly because you will inevitably find something better stats-wise and it feels like a waste to even bother with doing it.

I say the game is at odds with itself because it feels like despite being a pretty decent, good-but-not-great twin-stick shooter, it seems like it really wants to be an RPG and I would have loved that as well.  Obviously you have the levelling and stats progression so it's got the 'rpg elements' down pat, but you can also get into the pause menu to find that there's just a metric ton of lore and data to read that really builds up this wonderful dystopian cyberpunk world.  None of it is required reading and in my few hours with the game, it never told me that it was even there in the first place.  I'm talking "Mass Effect planet descriptions" levels of world building that would feel right at home in an RPG.  Not saying that it doesn't work with this genre, either, but it feels like it should be telling a much more complex and deeper story that wouldn't quite feel so at home here; and the story we get does well enough, but I personally just feel lost potential here.  Maybe a spiritual spin-off could happen.

In any case, The Ascent doesn't demand too much of your cash so we should fairly temper our expecations.  What it does well, it does exceedingly well and deserves accolades.  Where it lacks, it only does so in the realm of tolerance in that while it could be better, what's here is still fun to play and explore.  It's wide-open and you can find yourself wandering into dangerous places if you're not careful.  It's probably better co-op, but I wouldn't know.

(+) Absolutely amazingly detailed world with great worldbuilding to boot (This is pretty much the main selling point of the game)
(+) Gameplay is great and addicting (for the first couple of hours)
(+) Quite a few customization options with the use of transmog (not a big game, so not expecting much)
(+) Runs buttery smooth 90% of the time on my mid end laptop
(+) Decent 25+ hours game for a relatively cheap price
(+) Some absolutely fun to use augmentations (LASERS!) and abilities (POCKET MECHS!)

(-) Story is pretty basic, characters are all forgettable (except for my boy noghead)
(-) Very simplistic mission designs 
(-) Several crashes and bugs (like getting stuck under an enemy mech)
(-) Gameplay starts to overstay its' welcome and becomes repetitive by the last third of the campaign
(-) Checkpoints in this game are absolutely shit, died half of the way in this incredibly long section? Do it all over again.
(-) Meant to be played with friends, you're going to die lots of times playing alone due to massive enemy density in later areas 
(-) Lots, and I mean lots, of walking around, which is basically 60% of the game, with enemies littered throughout the map, I personally wasn't too bothered by this, but this will be off putting for many
(-) This game softlocks itself from time to time by giving you sidequests to places that is inaccessible until you've progressed far enough in the campaign (it also won't tell you that you don't have access to these places yet either)

In the end, I still personally enjoyed it, will probably forget it in a couple of months, but it was still pretty fun. (6,5/10)

Not bad.  Not bad.  
Probably about a 6/10 sort of game. And believe me, that isn't bad. Isn't great either though. 
I'll break it down... 

~ [b]Pros[/b] ~
+ : Pretty, for an isometric.  Didn't feel like most of those janky indie games trying to be "artistic" as an excuse for cartoony graphics.
+ : Mostly smooth gameplay.  I didn't get any game jitters.  My GPU was safe the whole time. 
+ : Grimdark.  Not quite as grimdark as Hatred, but still pretty grimdark. Can kill random people freely and the game only chastises me for it.  Even for opening fire with an automatic weapon in a nightclub.  What I'm saying is that it was fun for a violence-loving libertine like myself.  All the moreso thanks to the free DLC that let me do it with a reindeer head.
+ : Gear transmog, which is unusual.  In fact I haven't seen it outside of the recent MH games.  It let me keep the reindeer head for the entire game. Yay!
+ : The taxi fast-travel saves a lot of time, at least within a single level.  Not quite so convenient to get to the lifts between levels though.  Also saved me from the void twice, which is... something.
+ : Nothing too obscure or unintuitive that you'd never find it.  The important stuff is either located on the map or made apparent through minimap markers and random dialogue comments. 
+ : Found a few cool Bladerunner references.  Well, quite a lot actually, but then it seems to be THE primary inspiration behind the game.
+ : The music reminds me of Mass Effect.  In fact most of the parts that didn't remind me of Bladerunner reminded me of Mass Effect instead. 


~ [b]Cons[/b] ~
- : No Run option.  The only real way of getting around quickly is to equip that Javelin Dash module, max out the Evasion attribute, and then dodge everywhere.  Really.   The movement speed is slow as chilled molasses otherwise. 
- : No branching.  No choices.  No replay value.  While the map has you go about in all sorts of directions and backtrack a lot, the "plot" is linear and not particularly interesting.  Play through the game once with all the sidequests and you have done everything.  There isn't even enough variety in the build options to justify doing it again with different guns.
- : There are some pretty severe bugs. I didn't see any of the absolutely game-breaking bugs others spoke of...  but twice during the course of the game I was dumped out into the void at the top-middle of the game map after a cutscene and had to "taxi" just to get back to the game terrain.  Apparently the multiplayer is downright unplayable due to all the bugs, but I only touched it long enough to get the two related achievements.  I'm pretty sure bugs triggered some of the achievements early too.
- : There are certain characters I really wanted to kill.  I didn't get to.  I got badmouthed by these prats the entire game and aren't even allowed a mote of revenge.  For a game whose entire gameplay and plot is about being the hiveworld's best murder-hobo, that is a major shortcoming. 
- : The English voice-acting was awful.  At one point it even cut out entirely and I got treated to whatever the hell the game's original language dialogue was...  from that big guy whose voice sounded like he couldn't make up his mind whether to be bad Cockney or bad Scottish.  I'd have been fine with just the subtitles alone if that is how badly you're going to butcher things.  



Anyway... I had fun.  That was the most important thing.   Now I've got one achievement left to go:   
Die.  Lots.

I normally don't write reviews but I have a free hour while I am waiting on the ascent to load.

I have only been playing this game on 4 player multiplayer.
This is the buggiest game I have ever played, including dead island. Most of the game is spent on loading, crashing, stuck in menus or in the taxi. We had to turn it down to direct x 11 to reduce the crashing from every 5 minutes to every hour. Often the enemies don't bother turning up, breaking objectives. I have been attacked by hordes of T posing enemies multiple times per session. The ingame map and the map in the menu almost never loads. Loading times are abysmal. Enemy corpses often don't despawn. Flying enemies. Broken ragdolls. Multiple instances of PCs spawning in the taxi. Music is good except when it is continually cutting out.

The gameplay is fun for the first few hours but the bugs build up as you progress. This game should be really fun but ends up being a chore just to get the game to work.

If you are willing to play this game on ITS terms, then you might very well find a good time here. 

This game is gorgeous, first of all. A sprawling mess of habs and storefronts, littered with the detritus of a failed society. At several points during play on my Steam Deck, I'd toss Blade Runner, Blade Runner 2049, or Fifth Element on the TV in the background just to further enmesh myself. There are plenty of cyberpunk games out there, but few that are actually satisfying. The Ascent CAN be satisfying.

The issues are mechanical. You have very little control over what happens beyond shooting.  You don't have a save option, you don't have a map guide option.  You can pick which mission you are on, but that's it for navigation. The game auto-saves at seemingly random moments, usually after a mission but not always (and the time elapsed since last save option is not as useful as the devs think).  These are simple issues with no real reason to exist beyond strained resources and limited dev time, and definitely should have been addressed before the Cyber Heist was released.

I thoroughly enjoyed the story, which is RARE for a twin-stick style shooter. The Ascent Group going belly-up, then other Corp assets come in, your role with Poone, I found all of it highly engaging...at first.  By the end, it is very much a slog without much rhyme or reason, mostly static scenes of your character sitting in a taxi or elevator as you travel from point to point, and then simply just ends.  Then the Cyber Heist add-on begins...with a new area that is very difficult to navigate... and then it also just ends.

At this point I don't believe there is much left for me in the game, I've completed all the missions, collected all the weapons, done all the side missions (though several achievements seem to be broken and not triggering).  I wish there was more because the core game loop is fun.

Graphically stunning, but otherwise a bit mired. For anyone who loves either the cyberpunk setting or twin stick shooters, I would recommend it with the above caveats.

After playing the game a fair bit, I do not recommend it. It looks great, sounds great, but delivers a fairly shallow and very repetitive experience, made worse with backtracking, and riddled with frequent freezes and crashes in multiplayer.

The Pros:
+ The game absolutely nails the cyberpunk aesthetic, with tons of neat details in every environment.
+ Character visuals and stat distribution can be altered at hubs at any time.
+ The music tracks for combat encounters are simple, but good.
+ Competent voice acting for all missions-related NPCs, with a decent dose of humor.

The Cons:
- [b] The game is unstable, especially in co-op. [/b] Playing 4-man online coop, we could not complete a single mission without at least a couple freezes and crashes along the way - and individual missions are not long. It is bad enough that I would not recommend this game even if this was its only shortcoming.
- Almost all weapons play the same, with the differences boiling down to clip sizes, base reload speed and damage type (of which there are 4, but 2 of those are so rare/limited they might as well not exist) - possibly revving times for minigun-like weapons. A few weapons get perks like ricocheting bullets, extra fire damage or homing projectiles, but that is all.
- The game is trying to have a cover system, but a commonly used method for spawning in additional enemies is to simply have them step out of a portal (even street thugs and feral mutants!), often behind or next to the player, invalidating any cover they had. So you just run and gun most of the time.
- There is just ONE melee weapon option in the base game. In a world of augmented humans and aliens carrying huge hammers, electric stun batons, combat shields and katanas, you get a metal baseball bat.
- There are no meaningful character builds. The main differences between two characters boil down to which combat augments they equip, the rest is just flat stats boosting critical hit rate, reload speed, max health etc. In terms of gameplay experience, everyone is the same.
- Navigating the game world can be headache. The world has multiple levels and sub-areas, connected by elevators, bridges and stairs, which the stylized world map does not communicate well. There is also frequent backtracking, with combat encounters resetting between visits.

Love the game. Which they would of done more work on the coop side to make it playable with less crashes. Other then that its a great game that still gets us coming back for more every once in a while hoping they fixed the issues. Hmm it is hard to review this game.

- Graphically? It is stunning! Don't even get me started about the rain.
- Gameplay wise? Feels like Diablo 2 on steroids (with a "don't bother me" inventory system that is also pretty good). You just plow through enemies, sometimes facing challenges.
- Sound design is pretty good, the music is very depressing as any good Cyberpunk media
- Story... felt very unimportant... it was more like a "follow the waypoint" simulator.
- The camera angles and zoom are very limiting, sometimes even end up completely blocking you from properly fighting. 
- The map is far from decent, it is barely usable.

All that said, it almost feel like they missed an opportunity. But it is understandable as the requirements and budget for the game would be much higher. And what I mean by that is this universe almost begs to be a 3rd person or even 1st person game. Or at the bare minimum to have a free camera mode. Visually it is just too rich, I daresay it puts Cyberpunk 2077 to shame on how cyberpunk everything looks.

The Ascent is a Top-down Twinstick shooter story filled RPG. The lore of Ascent surrounding and world was phenomenally crafted and design, it was so immersive to every tiny little details. The shooting feel so satisfying! It feel punchy and pack...but the shortcoming overshadow and break this beautiful and immersive game. The Ascent somehow fall short on adrenaline action shooting and the RPG story such as the trailer advertised. You'll get some action here and there upon your mission or exploration but it get old and underwhelm quick.

The Gameplay,the Graphic and the Audio was one of the most stunning and the best! I've experience for a topdown shooter, it was so beautifully design to made this dystopian cyberpunk world look and sound so surreal with the eargasm soundtrack. Standing ovation and hat off to the dev on this. 

Alas, there is no escape for the shortcoming and disappointment in The Ascent. Rain upon rain of hailing bullets of the gamebreaking bugs and glitch upon the community was popping up here and there, Multiplayer was not that optimized, often over time there will be session of multiplayer that would corrupted player save files or had their game graphically bugged or glitched. This do happened to singleplayer experience as well! I myself experience the corrupted save file once! But lucky me I did manual backup thus my lost wasn't that bad compare to other....just merely 24 hours gameplay gone, others had worst.

I hope the dev can fix all the gamebreaking bug in shortest time and add more content to the gameplay in the future. Horde mode like The Helldivers™ would greatly welcome! It definitely will boost the sales and concurrent number of player. The Gamebreaking bug is really breaking the community apart and lastly the biggest letdown of all, the regional pricing doesn't justified the content. The game was too short and it deserve more for the current asking price. Do I recommend The Ascent?! Please, yes, please do grab a copy when it on sales but not on current full price to experience the phenomenal world of the Ascent.

The game looks very beautiful it really recreates the cyberpunk feel reminding of Ghost in the shell, Blade Runner and otehr classics. 
Sadly the game itself is very unstable. One hard lockup about every 1-2 hours and many other bugs (such as parts of the map not loading and such).

The game crashes frequently, freezes, and has UI bugs. If I try to open the map or travel too quickly while loading in, the game soft locks. In addition, the weapon upgrades don't feel impactful and the equipment variety is bland. The camera is not controllable and interferes with combat.

I freaking love this game. Brings me back to the old games from my childhood but with current-gen graphics!
None of that always-online nonesense or min-maxing bullshit!

The music is top notch. Audio and ambient is amazing, makes you feel like you're there and it's really living up to the cyberpunk genre. You can hear cop cars pass by you and the doppler effect is fantastic, you can tell when the car has passed!

I fukken love the music, did I say that already?

The combat music's so gritty and bass heavy, it makes me want to just jump in and splatter the enemies on the walls and floor.

The city feels alive, even if it's "diseased" by poverty, dirt and neglect. There's people going about their lives, ships flying around, drones buzzing overhead.

I like the fact that security just ignores you, that way if I misfire or my finger twitches I won't get my ass handed to me by corpsec.

Found only two bugs so far: enemies can attack you while you're talking to a quest giver so your options are to stay there and get shot or skip and miss the dialogue :( The other one happened after I took the fast-travel taxi and after disembarking my weapons would no longer consume ammo, so I didn't have to reload the weapons anymore. Fixed it by just going to main menu and then resuming the game.

The AI is pretty solid! If you move in a straight line they will lead you with their shots and hit you. Sometimes enemies dodge just as you're aiming at them and make you miss your shots, and almost always they'll try to surround or flank you. Civilians will run away from gun fights in the streets and sometimes they exlaim "Not this shit again!", it really adds to the cyberpunk and dystopian atmosphere.

It's a bummer that there's no sprint option, but at least you can dodge forward to move a liiitle bit faster.

There's not much in way of customizing weapons, you just upgrade them, but the weapon selection is pretty fair. Same goes for armor and augs.

Another cute little detail that I like is that you can turn off some of the corporations' ads when you walk past them.

It would've been nice to make hacking a bigger part of the gameplay, not just hacking doors, turrets and vending machines.

[h1]Tl;dr[/h1]
The Ascent is a visual marvel, offering an incredibly detailed cyberpunk / sci-fi urban environment to move through. Unfortunately, the rest of the game does not adhere to this high standard of quality, as gameplay, story and general user experience compare quite unfavorably to competitors in this genre (a shooter with RPG elements). Buy at your own risks.

[h1]Long version[/h1]
The Ascent is extremely impressive visually. The art direction works perfectly for this dirty, decadent, violent and futuristic setting. But what really shines is the sheer amount of visual detail and polish put into the environments. I don’t think I have ever seen such meticulously handcrafted game levels before. While playing, I often stopped just to look at the background. If there is one positive aspect that defines The Ascent and that is worth experiencing, this is it.

While it's obvious that the studio who made The Ascent is lead by a prolific and talented environmental artist, it is also obvious that this studio is lacking in terms of game design, UX and writing. And this is where things go south for The Ascent.

First, let’s talk about the story, which fails at being the link between the game world and the players. Each NPC you meet is basically the same hyperactive, long-winded talker and all that comes out of their mouth is overwrought techno-babble that assumes you want to study the lore of the game. After a while, you can’t help but skip, skip, skip, sadly. But the worse offender, is that the game makes no effort to weave your characters into the story: it’s the NPCs who are having their own convoluted story between themselves, while you’re like an outsider hired for FedEx missions. Hard to feel immersed or involved.

As for gameplay, I’ll start by saying that the basic action of shooting enemies is decent in this game. However, this mechanic is poorly supported by other systems. For instance, pacing is poor. There is a lot of walking in between the short missions, and so the same trash mobs have to be dealt with countless times, making the game feel repetitive and low in excitement. This is further increased by the fact that there is not much tactical elements to combat which results in all fights being essentially similar. And balancing of weapons and enemies is the opposite of smooth; you constantly feel like you don’t know why a fight was hard or easy.

Progression, which is typically the backbone of player retention, is quite unexciting here, because skills are all stat boosts, which means that they don’t lead to different builds or playing style. Weapons progression is equally bland, but it also suffers from an annoying contradiction: the game teaches you early on that you should upgrade weapon types with your precious upgrade resources, but then the game throws at you a ton of weapons of different types, which means you either ignore 90% of weapons to focus on upgrades, or you ignore upgrades to use a variety of weapons. Unsatisfying in both cases. 

Another offender is how obscure, unintuitive or badly explained many of the systems are. For example, the spec sheet for any weapon has 8 stats, a lot of them unexplained. And since it’s not clear what enemies are strong or weak against, choosing what to equip is a futile exercise, where you look at a whole lot of numbers, each of which can be higher or lower than your currently equipped piece. What a mess. Your special items (grenades and augments) also suffer from weird and obscure designs for how they recharge and become available again. So many other small things are also badly designed in menus, such as the act of selling extra loot at the store, which is stupidly tedious. And then there are things like when you are in the menus to equip something, nothing tells you if you start being shot at, so you can actually die cluelessly while in the menus. All in all, these numerous UX faux-pas don’t break the game, but it makes playing the Ascent much less enjoyable than it could have been.

And finally, the technical delivery of the game is far from flawless (at the time of writing this, which is a few weeks after release). Multiplayer has a lot of bugs, including disconnections, tutorials that keep popping every game session, HUD disappearing, various problems with starting group dialogue with NPCs, etc.

So all in all, a relatively bad game experience with very pretty environments.

The Ascent makes a strong first impression with its gorgeous cyberpunk visuals, dense environments, and gritty atmosphere. It's especially impressive considering it was developed by a team of just over ten people.

For a few glorious hours, I thought I’d found the Helldivers of Neon Grime—tactical, chaotic, and unashamedly over the top. Then I realized I was less liberating space and more weaving through waves of bland enemies and vending machines scattered across a crime-ridden corporate labyrinth. My optimism quietly bled out in a back alley, lost somewhere in a world I so badly wanted to love.

Fights become repetitive quickly, and enemy design is both lacklustre and uninspired. Combat lacks impact. Aiming is twitchy. I never really found my groove with it. The game adds complexity through cover mechanics, dodge rolls, and weapon variety, but none of it is enough to smooth over the rough edges or shake the lingering sense that I was playing a game still in early access.

Map design is confusing, and traversal is a chore, slowed by a snail-paced movement speed that turned my time into a test of patience. Side missions are mostly generic fetch quests with forgettable story lines, offering little to the world or the overall experience. Throughout, I had an overriding sense that my time wasn’t being respected.

The story is overly ambitious and didn’t resonate with me. I eventually lost interest and stopped trying to make sense of it. Its dystopian setup has potential, but weak writing and poor voice acting fail to bring the world to life. Despite a few compelling moments, the narrative feels convoluted and self-important, shedding emotional weight as it unfolds.

I didn’t personally enjoy the experience, but I still gave it a thumbs-up on Steam out of respect for what such a small dev team managed to accomplish. It’s unpolished and rough around the edges, but I can also see why it would (and does) appeal to many. I lost interest after a few hours—the completionist in me pushed through anyway. Buy it on a deep sale, but go in expecting a bumpy ride.

Update: I’ve changed this to a thumbs down. The endgame cleanup is a confusing, frustrating mess. I’m starting to think the map might actually be the real final boss.
